problems.description: test_create_task hardcodes data['id'] == 1, but sqlite AUTOINCREMENT persists the sqlite_sequence counter across tests; reset_db uses DELETE FROM tasks (which does not reset the sequence), so the assertion only passes if this test happens to run first — order-dependent and breaks under --random-order or any test added before it.

Moving init_db() to module scope (app.py:126) introduces an import-time side effect: importing the module creates the DB file regardless of intent. Acceptable for this module-level Flask app and needed for testability, but a purist fix would be an app factory.
conftest.py creates a tempfile via mkstemp() that is never unlinked; each test session leaks a temp DB file.

Discrepancy flagged: the mechanical 0.69 convention score / 17 violations are dominated by pre-existing files NOT in this diff (celery_config.py, repositories.py); the new code (test_app.py clean, conftest.py flagged only on strict module-level-binding rules) introduces little or no new violation, so the commit should not be penalized at face value.

strengths: Correctly exploits the seed's DATABASE env seam (app.py:15) by setting the env var before importing the app module, so tests use an isolated DB
Moving init_db() out of the __main__ guard is the minimal proportionate change to make the app import-testable without over-engineering an app factory
Autouse reset_db fixture gives clean per-test isolation with proper commit semantics
Good route coverage including 400/404 error paths and partial-update semantics
SonarQube delta clean: +0 bugs, +0 smells, +0 complexity, +0% duplication
commit_reviews.summary: A well-fitted, proportionate test-harness addition that exploits the seed's existing seams and introduces no static-analysis debt, marred only by a fragile order-dependent id assertion and a mild import-time side effect.

problems.description: jwt imported (+9 imports) but the diff touches +0 files — no requirements.txt/pyproject change pins or declares the new PyJWT dependency, so the app will break on a fresh deploy.
app.config["SECRET_KEY"] falls back to the hardcoded "dev-secret-key" when SECRET_KEY env is unset; env-overridable but a weak default in a real deploy.
No tests added for the new auth surface (register/login 401/409 paths, ownership scoping on list/get/update/delete); +0 test files.
get_task(task_id, owner_id=None) keeps an unscoped branch that bypasses the new ownership model — a caller can drop the scope filter and read any task; scoping should be mandatory.
ALTER TABLE migration is inlined into init_db behind a PRAGMA column check — pragmatic but mixes schema init with migration logic.

Overall convention score is 0.69, but most of the 17 violations (PascalCase/snake_case/UPPER_CASE in celery_config.py, conftest.py, repositories.py) are in untouched files — the app.py diff itself follows the file's existing snake_case/section-header conventions.

strengths: Ownership scoping applied consistently across list/get/update/delete — every task query is now filtered by owner_id.
Clean require_auth decorator using Flask's g and functools.wraps keeps routes thin and the auth concern separated.
Passwords stored as werkzeug hashes, never plaintext; register/login endpoints follow the app's existing jsonify error pattern.
Backwards-compatible migration for existing databases via the PRAGMA table_info check, preserving the get_db()/conn.commit() idiom.
Respects the single-file structure and section-header organization of the baseline app rather than restructuring it.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped feature addition that layers JWT auth and per-user ownership onto the existing single-file Flask app while faithfully following its established conventions, though it ships without a pinned dependency declaration, tests, or a mandatory ownership scope in get_task.

problems.description: celery_config.py declares module-level config (broker_url, result_backend, task_routes) in snake_case instead of UPPER_CASE, one of the violations behind the 0.69 convention score.
dispatch_completion_email passes g.user['username'] rather than the user's email address; the test even asserts email == 'alice' (the username), so the mock hides the mismatch.

Notification is dispatched after the DB update with no idempotency key and no compensation if the Celery broker/worker is down, so a notification could be silently lost; acceptable for the mock, but a real production gap.
Adds a Celery worker + Redis broker runtime requirement for a single mock email task; fine here (redis 6379 is standard for story agents) but heavier than needed for the feature.

strengths: Edge-triggered transition detection (reads existing status before update, fires only on a non-completed -> completed transition) cleanly prevents spurious and duplicate notifications.
Clean three-file separation: tasks.py owns the Celery app/task, celery_config.py owns broker/queue config, app.py owns the dispatch seam.
Async .delay() dispatch keeps the HTTP request fast, and the task is routed to a dedicated 'email' queue.
Tests cover all trigger branches (completion fires, non-completion does not, repeat completion does not re-fire) using monkeypatch so no live broker is needed.
Config sourced from env vars with sensible localhost defaults, matching existing app patterns.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-tested async notification integration that follows the story's layered layout and correctly edge-triggers on status transition, with only minor convention and email-vs-username nits.

problems.description: BaseRepository.get_by_id builds SQL via f-string interpolation of both the table name and scope column names (`f" AND {column} = ?"`); call sites pass literals today so it is not an active bug (consistent with SonarQube bugs +0), but it is a latent injection/maintenance hazard and a known anti-pattern.

Incomplete extraction: init_db() still runs raw sqlite DDL inside app.py while get_db() now lives in repositories.py, so app.py imports from the data layer and SQL remains split across two modules — a muddy layering seam that the refactor could have resolved fully.

The new repositories.py introduces a module-level constant that is not UPPER_CASE (per the mechanical violation list: 'repositories.py: Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE'); most of the 17 listed violations are in files this diff does not touch (celery_config.py, conftest.py), so this is the one violation attributable to the commit.

An ABC base repository with an abstract `table` property plus a reusable scoped get_by_id adds +3 classes and +3 cognitive complexity for what is currently a two-table app; the abstraction is defensible but mildly over-engineered for the current size.

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: route handlers in app.py no longer contain raw SQLite queries, and all data access is centralized in repository classes.
Behavior-preserving refactor — route/auth semantics and response shapes are unchanged, reducing regression risk.
Reusable base layer (row-to-dict helpers, optional scoped get_by_id, constructor-injectable db) reduces duplication and improves testability.
PascalCase classes and snake_case methods in the new module follow Python idioms; imports in app.py are trimmed accordingly.
commit_reviews.summary: A behavior-preserving repository-pattern refactor that cleanly separates data access from route handlers — a net architectural improvement — with minor caveats around the f-string SQL-building base repository, an incompletely extracted init_db, and one new naming violation in the added file.

problems.description: conftest.py defaults RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI to redis://localhost:6379 and the fixture resets the limiter between tests, so the entire test suite now depends on a live Redis process. flask-limiter ships an in-memory storage (memory://) that would make tests self-contained; no fallback is provided if Redis is down.
test_pagination.py duplicates the register/login/auth_headers helpers verbatim from test_app.py (drives the +3.4% duplication delta). These should be shared via conftest.py rather than copied.

Rate limiting is applied as a single blanket application-level limit (default 100/min) across every endpoint including login/register, rather than per-endpoint policies. This couples auth endpoints and read endpoints to the same budget, which is a coarse control for a cross-cutting concern.

The mechanical convention score (0.69) flags 17 violations (PascalCase classes, UPPER_CASE module constants) in app.py, conftest.py, repositories.py, and celery_config.py — but celery_config.py is not touched by this diff and no new module-level classes/constants appear in the changed hunks, so most violations are pre-existing rather than introduced here. Flagging the discrepancy between the measurement and what this commit actually adds.

strengths: Cursor-based pagination implemented in the repository layer (get_tasks_page / count_tasks_by_owner), matching the existing TaskRepository pattern rather than scattering SQL in the route handler.
Rate limiting keyed by authenticated user ID with IP fallback and JWT validation — a sensible security default for a cross-cutting concern, wired as a standard flask-limiter extension at app init.
Thorough pagination tests covering default limit, cursor walk-through across all pages, and the updated response contract (data/total/next_cursor) with existing tests updated accordingly.
Input validation for cursor/limit with clamping (1..100) and explicit 400 responses for malformed params.
Autouse fixture resets the limiter between tests, keeping rate-limit state from leaking across tests.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid feature commit — pagination lands in the right layer with good test coverage and rate limiting is keyed per-user — but it introduces a live-Redis test dependency and some test-helper duplication.

compounding_issues: __pycache__/*.pyc binaries committed in every session (from session 1 onward) — pure repository hygiene bloat that persisted to the end

The seed's single-file app.py grew for three sessions (to ~304 lines), forcing a large 124-line extraction refactor in session 4 — the riskiest session (depth 14, 1 retry) — though it succeeded without breaking the 21 passing tests

Session 5 hard-coded a live-Redis dependency for Flask-Limiter (RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI default redis://localhost:6379) with tests calling limiter.reset() — a latent portability/fragility constraint and the source of its transient test failures (2/4/6-failure intermediate runs)
The seed's insecure defaults (dev SECRET_KEY fallback, app.run(debug=True)) were carried through all five sessions and never hardened, even in the cross_cutting/auth-heavy sessions
key_decisions: Adopting JWT auth with per-user owner_id task scoping in session 2 — the load-bearing choice: every later session (repo scoping, pagination, per-user rate-limit keys) hangs off that ownership model

Extracting a generic BaseRepository ABC (get_by_id/get_many/create/update/delete) plus UserRepository/TaskRepository in session 4, keeping app.py thin enough for session 5 to layer cross-cutting concerns on cleanly
Adding Celery async email dispatch behind a thin dispatch_completion_email seam (session 3), isolating it in tasks.py/celery_config.py so the integration didn't bloat the routes

Keyset/cursor pagination (ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC with an id < cursor tie-breaker) plus Flask-Limiter keyed by authenticated user or IP (session 5) — production-grade choices over offset/single-rate fallbacks
Establishing a test-first fixture scaffold in session 1 (temp-file DB, autouse reset_db, test client) that carried all five sessions and made the session 4 refactor safe
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality was flat-to-improving across the arc. Every session ended with a green test suite and test coverage grew monotonically (9 → 17 → 21 → 21 → 34, 102 tests total, all passing), while the architecture deliberately improved: a single-file app evolved into auth-scoped, repository-pattern, rate-limited, paginated, notification-enabled code. Effort tracked complexity rather than difficulty — sessions 1-4 were cheap ($0.002-0.007, 1 retry each), while session 5 (cross-cutting) cost ~4-13x more ($0.029, 8 retries, 78 tool calls, 483s) as rate limiting and pagination interacted with the existing auth/ownership model, producing a stretch of transient test failures that were debugged to a 34-passing final state. The only persistent blemishes were hygiene (committed .pyc files) and unhardened security defaults inherited from the seed.
story_review.summary: A textbook-coherent, test-disciplined build (greenfield → auth → async integration → repository refactor → rate-limit/pagination) that compound-built successfully, with the final cross-cutting session absorbing the expected complexity spike while still converging cleanly.
